children: Bullion starts November higher, but rate-hike expectations and last week’s forced-selling concerns leave the recovery facing an early test.
📈 Gold rebounds after October’s heavy losses
Gold climbed roughly 0.9% to $3,911 an ounce early Monday, recovering some ground after falling 6.8% in October.
The bounce offers relief following a difficult month, although bullion remains below $4,000—a clear reference point for traders assessing whether buyers can sustain the recovery.

Friday’s selloff pushed spot gold to its lowest level since October 2025. Bullion fell about 4% to $3,870 during the session, while December futures settled at $3,898. A market usually associated with shelter proved vulnerable when investors needed cash elsewhere.
Analysts pointed to possible forced selling during the

. Investors facing margin calls — demands for additional collateral on leveraged positions — may sell liquid holdings such as gold to raise cash. That helps explain how bullion can fall alongside stocks even during heightened uncertainty.
🛢️ Cheaper oil offers some inflation relief

Oil retreated sharply Monday while diplomatic talks continued over Iran. Brent fell more than 3% toward $109.70, with WTI near $100.58. Easing energy prices could temper inflation concerns and reduce pressure for higher interest rates, although continued tanker attacks leave supply risks unresolved.

The rate outlook remains a significant obstacle. Markets assigned roughly a three-in-four probability to a December Fed hike. Gold pays no interest, so higher yields on cash and bonds increase the income investors forgo by holding it, making a sustained recovery more demanding.

Treasury yields have eased considerably from October’s highs, with the US 10-year around 4.93% Monday. That offers a more supportive backdrop for bullion, but the next move depends partly on incoming data: renewed yield increases could quickly challenge the metal’s tentative rebound.
🔎 Jobs data puts the recovery to the test
Friday’s US employment report is the week’s main macro checkpoint. Stronger hiring could reinforce expectations of tighter monetary policy, while weaker figures could ease them.
Gold traders will watch the dollar and Treasury-market reaction alongside the headline jobs number for evidence of changing rate expectations.
Before payrolls, the calendar brings several opportunities for volatility. US ISM manufacturing arrives Monday, followed by Tuesday’s midterm elections and Wednesday’s ISM services report.
The RBA and Bank of England also decide rates this week, keeping global inflation and borrowing costs in focus.

Silver joined Monday’s recovery, rising roughly 2% toward $50 an ounce. A stronger recovery for both metals would need follow-through beyond the initial bounce, particularly if rate-hike expectations remain elevated.
